name: Sound Physics
title: Sound Engineer
blurb: A hands-on physics side-skill that sharpens Arin's quantitative reasoning (logs, ratios, sampling) with instant feedback through the ears.

chapters.title: Waves, frequency and wavelength
chapters.read: An introductory physics or audio-engineering textbook's chapter on sound waves: longitudinal waves, frequency, period, wavelength, the speed of sound (about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C) and the range of human hearing.
chapters.produce: Build a small table (spreadsheet or by hand) of wavelength and period for 20 Hz, 100 Hz, 1 kHz, 10 kHz and 20 kHz, and use a free tone-generator app to test the top of your own hearing range.

quiz.q: With the speed of sound at 343 m/s, what is the wavelength of a 686 Hz tone?
With the speed of sound at 343 m/s, what is the wavelength of a 100 Hz bass note?
What is the period of a 250 Hz tone, in milliseconds?
What kind of wave is sound travelling through air?
opts: Longitudinal: air particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel
Transverse: particles move at right angles to the direction of travel
quiz.ex: Sound in air is a series of compressions and rarefactions along the direction of propagation.

quiz.q: What is the commonly quoted frequency range of young, healthy human hearing?
quiz.ex: The textbook range is 20 Hz–20 kHz; the upper limit falls with age.

quiz.q: With the speed of sound at 343 m/s, what frequency has a wavelength of 0.1715 m?

chapters.title: Decibels and loudness
chapters.read: An audio-engineering textbook's chapter on decibels: logarithms, dB SPL, 10·log10 for power and intensity vs 20·log10 for pressure, adding incoherent sources, the inverse-square law and equal-loudness contours.
chapters.produce: Write a one-page dB cheat sheet with worked examples (adding two sources, doubling distance, pressure vs power ratios) and check three of them with a free sound-level-meter app.

quiz.q: Two equal, uncorrelated sound sources each produce 80 dB SPL at a listening point. What is the combined level? (2 decimal places)
For a point source in a free field, by how many dB does the level drop when you double your distance from it? (2 decimal places)
quiz.ex: Inverse-square law: 20·log10(2) ≈ 6.02 dB per doubling of distance.

quiz.q: Two uncorrelated sources produce 90 dB and 80 dB SPL at the same point. What is the combined level? (2 decimal places)
Roughly how much louder does a 10 dB increase sound to most listeners?
quiz.ex: +10 dB is 10× the power, but perceived loudness roughly doubles.

quiz.q: Equal-loudness contours show that human hearing at moderate levels is most sensitive around…
quiz.ex: Ear canal resonance boosts the 2–5 kHz region, so quiet sounds there are heard most easily.

quiz.q: By what factor does sound pressure increase when the level rises by 20 dB SPL?
quiz.ex: Pressure uses 20·log10: 20 dB → 10^(20/20) = 10×.

chapters.title: Harmonics and timbre
chapters.read: An acoustics or synthesis textbook's chapters on the harmonic series, standing waves in strings and pipes, waveform shapes (sine, square, sawtooth), envelopes (ADSR) and why instruments playing the same note sound different.
chapters.produce: Record the same note on two instruments or voices, view both in a free spectrum-analyser app, and write a short note comparing their harmonic content and envelopes.

quiz.q: A note has a fundamental of 110 Hz. What is the frequency of its third harmonic?
quiz.ex: The nth harmonic is n × fundamental: 3 × 110 = 330 Hz.

quiz.q: Two instruments play the same pitch at the same loudness but sound different. The difference is mainly due to…
opts: The speed of sound in the room
quiz.ex: Timbre comes from the mix of overtones and how the sound starts, sustains and decays.

quiz.q: An ideal square wave contains…
opts: Only odd harmonics, with amplitudes falling as 1/n
quiz.ex: A square wave = fundamental + 3rd, 5th, 7th… harmonics at 1/3, 1/5, 1/7… amplitude.

quiz.q: A pipe is open at both ends and 0.7 m long. With the speed of sound at 343 m/s, what is its fundamental frequency?
quiz.ex: Open–open pipe: f = v/(2L) = 343/1.4 = 245 Hz.

quiz.q: In an ADSR envelope, what does the S stand for, and what does it set?
opts: Sustain: how long the note takes to fade after release
Speed: how fast the attack is
Sustain: the level held while the note is held
Saturation: how much distortion is added
quiz.ex: Sustain is a level, not a time; Attack, Decay and Release are times.

quiz.q: A small speaker cannot reproduce 55 Hz, yet listeners still hear a 55 Hz pitch when it plays harmonics at 110, 165 and 220 Hz. This is called…
quiz.ex: The brain infers the fundamental from the spacing of the harmonics.

chapters.title: Room acoustics
chapters.read: An acoustics or home-studio guide's chapters on reflections, absorption vs diffusion, reverberation time and the Sabine formula, room modes (standing waves) and comb filtering.
chapters.produce: Measure a room you use (your apartment or a practice room), calculate its first three axial modes for each dimension, and write a short treatment plan saying where absorption or bass traps would help most.

quiz.q: A room is 5 m long. With the speed of sound at 343 m/s, what is the frequency of its first axial mode along that length?
Using Sabine's formula RT60 = 0.161 × V / A, what is the reverberation time of a 200 m³ room with total absorption A = 40 m² (sabins)?
What is the main difference between absorption and diffusion?
opts: Absorption turns sound energy into heat; diffusion scatters reflections in many directions
Absorption reflects sound back in one direction; diffusion turns it into heat
Both remove the same amount of sound energy
quiz.ex: Absorbers reduce reflected energy; diffusers keep the energy but spread it out.

quiz.q: Why do thin foam panels do little to fix boomy bass in a small room?
opts: Low frequencies have long wavelengths that need thick or specialised absorbers (bass traps)
Bass is not affected by rooms
quiz.ex: A 50 Hz wave is about 7 m long; thin porous material only absorbs much shorter wavelengths.

quiz.q: A rapid 'pinging' repeat heard when clapping between two parallel bare walls is called…
quiz.ex: Sound bouncing repeatedly between parallel reflective surfaces creates flutter echo.

quiz.q: A wall reflection travels 1.715 m further than the direct sound before reaching a microphone (speed of sound 343 m/s). At what frequency is the first comb-filter notch?
quiz.ex: Delay = 1.715/343 = 5 ms; first notch at 1/(2 × 0.005) = 100 Hz.

chapters.title: Digital audio: sampling and bit depth
chapters.read: An audio-engineering or DSP primer's chapters on sampling, the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, aliasing and anti-aliasing filters, quantisation and bit depth, dither, and PCM data rates.
chapters.produce: Export the same short recording at different sample rates and bit depths in a free audio editor, compare file sizes with your own calculations, and note what you can and cannot hear.

quiz.q: What is the Nyquist frequency for audio sampled at 48 kHz?
quiz.ex: Nyquist = sample rate / 2 = 48,000/2 = 24,000 Hz.

quiz.q: Using the rule of thumb of 6.02 dB per bit, what is the theoretical dynamic range of 16-bit audio? (2 decimal places)
What is the data rate of uncompressed stereo PCM audio at 44.1 kHz and 16 bits, in kbit/s?
A 30 kHz tone reaches an ADC sampling at 48 kHz with no anti-aliasing filter. At what frequency does the alias appear?
quiz.ex: Frequencies above Nyquist fold back: 48 − 30 = 18 kHz.

quiz.q: Why does an ADC need an anti-aliasing filter before sampling?
opts: To boost the bass before recording
To remove the DC offset after playback
To remove content above the Nyquist frequency so it cannot fold back as false tones
quiz.ex: A low-pass filter stops frequencies the sample rate cannot represent from aliasing into the audible band.

quiz.q: When reducing bit depth (e.g. 24-bit to 16-bit), dither is…
opts: Low-level noise added so quantisation error becomes benign noise instead of distortion
A filter that removes frequencies above Nyquist
A compressor that raises quiet sounds
A way to increase the sample rate
quiz.ex: Dither decorrelates quantisation error from the signal, trading distortion for a small noise floor.

chapters.title: EQ, compression and mixing basics
chapters.read: A mixing guide's chapters on equalisers (high-pass, shelf, bell; frequency, gain, Q), dynamics processors (threshold, ratio, attack, release, make-up gain), masking, panning and gain staging.
chapters.produce: Mix a free multitrack session (many are offered for practice): high-pass where needed, compress the vocal, carve space for kick and bass, and write a short log of every change and why.

quiz.q: A compressor has a threshold of −20 dBFS and a ratio of 4:1. A peak arrives at −8 dBFS. What is the output level of that peak (no make-up gain)?
quiz.ex: Over threshold by 12 dB; 12/4 = 3 dB over at the output, so −20 + 3 = −17 dBFS.

quiz.q: Why is a high-pass filter often put on a vocal track?
opts: To make the vocal brighter by boosting treble
To remove low-frequency rumble and handling noise the voice does not need
quiz.ex: Cutting below roughly 80–100 Hz removes mud and noise without hurting the voice.

quiz.q: On a bell (peaking) EQ, increasing the Q value makes the boost or cut…
opts: Shift to a higher centre frequency
quiz.ex: Q is the ratio of centre frequency to bandwidth, so higher Q = narrower band.

quiz.q: What does a compressor's attack time control?
opts: How quickly gain returns to normal after the signal falls below the threshold
The level at which compression begins
How much the output is boosted afterwards
How quickly gain reduction starts after the signal exceeds the threshold
quiz.ex: Attack = reaction time; release = recovery time; threshold = where it starts; make-up = post-gain.

quiz.q: A compressor has a threshold of −18 dBFS and a ratio of 3:1. An input peak at −6 dBFS is compressed. How many dB of gain reduction are applied?
quiz.ex: 12 dB over → 12/3 = 4 dB over at the output; gain reduction = 12 − 4 = 8 dB.

quiz.q: Two instruments occupy the same frequency range and blur together. This effect is called…
quiz.ex: Louder sounds hide quieter ones nearby in frequency; EQ cuts and panning reduce masking.

boss.q: With the speed of sound at 343 m/s, what is the wavelength of a 20 Hz tone? (2 decimal places)
Three equal, uncorrelated sources each give 60 dB SPL at a point. What is the combined level? (2 decimal places)
What is the minimum sample rate, in theory, needed to capture frequencies up to 22 kHz?
boss.ex: Nyquist: sample rate must be at least 2 × 22 = 44 kHz.

boss.q: Why are common sample rates such as 44.1 kHz and 48 kHz slightly more than twice 20 kHz?
opts: Human hearing extends to 24 kHz for most adults
They leave room for a practical anti-aliasing filter to roll off between 20 kHz and the Nyquist frequency
boss.ex: Real filters need a transition band; the gap above 20 kHz gives them space.

boss.q: How many distinct quantisation levels does 8-bit audio have?
A room is 4 m wide. With the speed of sound at 343 m/s, what is the frequency of the second axial mode across that width? (2 decimal places)
How does a sawtooth wave's harmonic content differ from a square wave's?
opts: A sawtooth contains only odd harmonics; a square wave contains all
A sawtooth contains all integer harmonics; a square wave contains only odd ones
A sawtooth contains only even harmonics
boss.ex: Both fall off as 1/n, but the sawtooth includes even harmonics too, giving a brighter, buzzier sound.

boss.q: A compressor has threshold −24 dBFS, ratio 2:1 and +4 dB make-up gain. An input peak arrives at −12 dBFS. What is the output level?
boss.ex: 12 dB over → 6 dB over at output: −24 + 6 = −18; add 4 dB make-up → −14 dBFS.

boss.q: According to Sabine's formula, which change will shorten a room's reverberation time?
opts: Making the room larger while keeping the same absorption
Raising the volume of the music
Adding absorptive material to the walls
boss.ex: RT60 = 0.161 V/A, so more absorption (larger A) reduces RT60.

boss.q: A kick drum and a bass guitar both crowd the 60–100 Hz region and the low end sounds muddy. Which first step fits standard mixing practice?
opts: Give each its own space, e.g. cut the bass slightly where the kick's fundamental sits (and vice versa)
Boost both at the same frequency
boss.ex: Complementary EQ reduces masking so each instrument is heard clearly.
